claim: Do not put design questions to the owner: a mechanism comes from the recorded research or the literature, a parameter is computed from measurements, a missing fact is measured; he is shown results and reasoning, not choices.
when: before asking the owner anything about how something should work or what value to use
quote: How would my opinion weigh more than proven algorithms and cs theory?

claim: A parameter (fault budget, time limit, alert path, how much memory, time and tokens a check may take) is the result of an optimisation against the objective, never the owner's preference; a number of his that would make the system worse is argued with, not obeyed.
when: before setting any limit, threshold, timeout or budget
quote: the optimal parameters are not decided by what my favorite one is

claim: The objective is fixed: quality first, then the least time, memory and tokens. Work is judged by seven measures: throughput, efficiency, token count, token cost, time taken, quality, hallucinations. Tokens are reported, never money.
evidence: CLAUDE.md#What every piece of work is judged by

claim: A test, review or model run happens only if its result can change what is done next: one attack round per fix, no re-run of unchanged work, no wide matrix, the full suite once at the end of a change.
when: before running or proposing any test, review, attack round or model run
quote: we also want to avoid useless extensive testing that wastes a shit ton of our time

when: before starting any helper or child session

claim: Open the recorded research from the files before designing or deciding. Do not work from session memory or from a note index. A compaction is not an excuse.
when: at the start of a session and before any design decision

claim: Hooks or scripts: no fixed preference. Hooks where hooks work best, scripts where scripts work best, or both. Look at every scenario before forming a view, including scripts acting in the middle of a session.
when: before choosing how a rule is enforced
quote: Don't take my opinion as an absolute truth. Where hooks work best, we use hooks. Where scripts work best, we use scripts.

claim: 'One writer per file' is rejected as the coarsest lock there is. Several writers on one file is a solved problem of concurrency control and is designed from that body of work.
when: before planning parallel writers
quote: you just resorted to, okay, let's just keep one writer

claim: A process writing shared memory and an agent writing a shared file are the same problem: use the core literature of concurrency and parallel computing, not only papers about AI agents.
when: before a literature search on anything agents do in parallel
quote: An agent writing something or a process writing something is kind of the same thing, is it not?

claim: Literature must be strong (reputable venues, high impact) and read in full. A blocked page is not the end: find the open copy by another route. A figure a decision rests on is quoted from the paper, not taken from a summary.

quote: not just giving up if we see a login page

claim: The bottleneck is not fixed: CPU, memory, tokens or the check can each be the limit, alone or together, depending on the workload. The design is a rule that finds the current bottleneck and routes to the method that fits it. Never design from one measured run.
when: before choosing a concurrency or scheduling method, and before generalising from a measurement
quote: it becomes mainly a decision problem as well, to route the most optimal methods towards the bottleneck

claim: The research tree's trusted scripts are built: 31 stages, 20,560 lines in the main scripts, suite 965 pass and 0 fail, end-to-end 232 of 232.
Thirteen fixes and one shared primitive (0b) for faults in those scripts are designed and none is built. There has been no pilot and no run of the tree.

One run of the tree's test suite takes 596 s (1,018 tests: 965 pass, 53 skipped), with one test file at a time (--test-concurrency=1), peak memory 494 MB, peak 12 processes, and about 3 of 24 threads busy on average. It was one run; whether test files can run side by side is not tested.
Heavy commands run one at a time through research-tree/tools/lane.mjs. Over 778 logged commands they ran 355 minutes and waited about 177 minutes in that queue.

In this app a hook does refuse a call: a write outside an allowed folder and a helper started on a refused model were both stopped, also with permissions bypassed; hooks fire for tool calls inside a helper, with the same session id and an agent id that tells the helper apart.

A hook's input carries session_id, transcript_path, tool_use_id, the tool's input (for Write the full content; for Agent the subagent_type and model when they are passed) and inside a helper agent_id and agent_type. The context size is not given to a hook. One hook call costs about 37 ms on this PC.

Nothing enforces any rule today: no hook is configured on this PC, the tree's guard hook and audit script are built but not installed, and the one mechanical limit is autoCompactWindow 400000 for Opus only.
The model named in an agent definition does not hold by itself: the documentation says the caller's own model value comes first. A hook, a deny rule or a workflow script can fix the model.

A session can start another session only on a turn the owner typed, or on the turn that follows one of its own sessions ending; it is refused on a turn begun by a helper's notice. A folder outside the project must be passed with backslashes. The stand-alone command-line program has no login; the login is in the desktop app.

To read a paper itself on this PC: download with curl -s -L --ssl-no-revoke (a plain download fails with exit 35), check the file starts with %PDF-, then pdftotext paper.pdf paper.txt and search the text. The fetch tool only returns a summary and the Read tool cannot render a PDF here.

For the 14 units to build: locked by file, 3 can be built at once; locked by function or block, 7 (8 with 0b first). They share 20 places: 9 are separate entries, keys or parts, 7 are ordered sequences, 4 change the same statements. Counted from the change list, not from diffs.

The build is 14 units: 4 large (FX-OUT, FX-CLAIM, FX-CGATE, FX-W4), 8 medium, 2 small; 12 scripts and thresholds.json change; 52 tests to add; 21 facts about the app that the designs lean on. Sizes are estimates from the change list.
Against the designs selected on 2026-11-16, no fix uses a different design: 9 use the recorded design and 5 use another variant of the same family (FX-OUT, FX-CLOSE, FX-PLAN, FX-W2, FX-W5).

Its measurements are real, but its token ceilings were measured in October on a smaller plan, and its own refuter put the best number of lanes near two.

The Horthy sweep kept 78 of 861 idea families (24 adopt, 54 trial). 9 carry a measured figure, 6 of them Horthy's own, none a controlled before and after. It does not settle how instruction files are laid out across a repository, and nothing from it was ever tried here.
'38 of 71' counts ideas the earlier build had practised that failed, mostly as lines in briefs and model re-checks; some script ideas failed too. It is not a comparison of prose against scripts.
'Hooks stay off' was never ruled: it is decision D17 of the harness v2 design, with a lean and no answer from the owner.

Agrawal, Carey and Livny 1987: whether optimistic control beats locking turns on resources. Locking wins when resources are scarce; optimistic control wins when they are plentiful. No paper read gives one conflict rate at which they cross.

Khanna, Kunal and Pierce 2007: three-way merge (diff3) is guaranteed clean only under stated conditions on the edited regions, and lacks several properties one would expect. Where more than two writers change one function the guarantee does not cover it.

Bailis and others 2014: operations that preserve the invariants under merge need no coordination (invariant confluence); ten of twelve invariants of their benchmark needed none. Their table says which kinds of change merge without coordination and which do not.

Operational transformation is ruled out for more than two writers: all five algorithms that Boucheneb and Imine checked fail to converge with three or more sites. A merge done by a model is the same kind of method and untested.

Measured on human teams: merges conflict textually in 16 % (Brun and others) and 7.6 to 19.3 % (Kasi and Sarma) of cases; a clean merge then fails the build in 1 % and the tests in 6 % (Brun), or the tests in 5.6 to 35 % (Kasi).

Shortening the serial check, measured elsewhere: Facebook runs a third of its tests and still catches 99.9 % of faulty changes; Ekstazi cuts test time by 32 % on average and 54 % on long suites; at Google 1.23 % of tests ever fail; Uber's main branch was green 52 % of the time before a merge queue.

Universal Scalability Law (Gunther): throughput peaks at N* = sqrt((1 - alpha) / beta) workers, confirmed in his own text and on his measured fits; one fitted case predicted a peak of 12,000 threads where 2,000 was measured, so the law needs a first measurement before it predicts.

Studies of AI agents changing one repository at once report textual conflicts in 20 to 42 % of pairs, and parallel agents between 21 % faster and 39 % slower. These figures were read from summaries only.

Several writers on one file: build 0b first; one small 'skeleton' change fixes the interfaces and turns each ordered sequence into a list of empty steps, one per fix; each fix fills its own steps on its own copy, in its own file where a function is shared; one script merges and tests. Not tried. Its choice between locking and optimistic writing assumes tokens are scarce and the PC is not, from one run: that must become a rule by bottleneck (r57-0015).

Enforcement is a mix: a workflow script fixes model and parallel start by construction; a hook or a deny rule stops a call inside a session; a script checks at plan, commit and merge; an audit of the transcript catches the rest. A question in plain text and work outside a session's purpose cannot be stopped by either.
The suite could run test files side by side, cutting one run from 596 s to about the longest file (about 270 s). Not tested: nobody knows whether the test files are independent.
